about: This is the complete TIH Financial Literacy Professional Certificate, rebuilt into ten modules that take you from the basics to financial confidence.

Every content lesson has a video and printable notes; downloadable templates cover a Monthly Budget, Savings Tracker, Investment Worksheet and a Personal Financial Plan guide. A capstone builds your own real financial plan.

Software & tools: Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets, ChatGPT, Google Finance, mobile banking and budgeting apps. You finish with a personal financial plan and — after the graduation assessment — a Certificate of Completion.
requirements: A notebook or a spreadsheet (Excel/Google Sheets) to practise
Your own real numbers to apply the lessons

faqs.question: Is this course really free?
faqs.answer: Yes, 100% free. TIH believes financial literacy is a basic life skill every Liberian deserves, regardless of income. There are no hidden fees and no credit card is required.

faqs.question: I don't have a bank account or much money. Can I still benefit?
faqs.answer: Absolutely, this course is designed for you. It starts with skills that need no bank account: goal setting, budgeting, expense tracking, mobile money safety, and susu savings. Banking is covered step by step for when you are ready.

faqs.question: Does the course use Liberian examples or foreign ones?
faqs.answer: Every module is grounded in Liberian reality: budgeting across USD and LRD, Orange Money and Lonestar Cell MTN MoMo, susu clubs, Monrovia market trading, and banking requirements in Liberia. Video lessons are supplemented with locally focused reading notes.

faqs.question: How long does it take and is the certificate recognized?
faqs.answer: Most learners finish in 3-4 weeks studying about an hour a day. Your TIH certificate includes a unique verification code (TIH-2026-FIN-0001 series) that employers, NGOs, and microfinance institutions can confirm online.

🧭 What is Financial Literacy?

This lesson explains What is Financial Literacy? so you can understand money decisions, goals, income, expenses, habits, and the foundation of financial well-being. It teaches the definition, calculation or comparison method, risks, and a complete example.

Money decision framework
🧭 What is Financial Literacy?
1. Know
2. Plan
3. Act
4. Review
Amount • timing • total cost • risk • evidence

Definition

Financial literacy is the knowledge and practical ability to make informed decisions about income, spending, saving, borrowing, risk protection, investing, and financial goals.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

What is Financial Literacy?

Financial literacy is the knowledge and practical ability to make informed decisions about income, spending, saving, borrowing, risk protection, investing, and financial goals.

financial literacy

the knowledge and practical ability to make informed decisions about earning, spending, saving, borrowing, protecting, and investing money

net worth

the value of assets minus liabilities

total cost

the full amount paid or used after including price, interest, fees, taxes, maintenance, and other relevant costs

Detailed explanation

Financial literacy is the knowledge and practical ability to make informed decisions about income, spending, saving, borrowing, risk protection, investing, and financial goals. A sound decision compares the full amount, timing, total cost, uncertainty, access to money, legal terms, and effect on other goals. Records and provider documents matter more than advertising claims.

  • Separate facts from assumptions and promises.
  • Compare at least two realistic options using the same period and basis.
  • Protect essential needs and emergency resilience before taking avoidable risk.
  • Review the plan when income, prices, responsibilities, laws, or goals change.

Step-by-step method

  1. Know: define the goal, amount, timing, obligations, and information needed.
  2. Plan: collect statements, contracts, rates, fees, risks, and current rules from reliable sources.
  3. Act: calculate and compare realistic options, including difficult scenarios.
  4. Review: choose deliberately, keep records, monitor results, and revise when evidence changes.

Worked real-life example

A learner lists monthly income, essential expenses, debts, savings, responsibilities, and goals before choosing a realistic next action.

Worked calculation

MeasureMethodExample
Monthly balanceIncome − expensesUS$300 − US$250 = US$50
Savings rateSavings ÷ income × 100US$50 ÷ US$300 × 100 = 16.7%

Check: State currency, period, rate basis, fees, assumptions, and rounding. Provider contracts and current local rules control real transactions.

Common mistakes and corrections

  • Mistake: focusing only on the monthly payment. Correction: compare total repayment, fees, rate, term, penalties, and collateral.
  • Mistake: treating every financial product as guaranteed. Correction: check risk, regulation, provider identity, contract, and loss scenarios.
  • Mistake: mixing personal and business money. Correction: separate accounts, records, budgets, and decisions.
  • Mistake: sharing PINs or one-time codes. Correction: keep credentials private and use official support channels.

Guided practice with detailed answer

Question: How should a learner apply What is Financial Literacy? when monthly income is limited and expenses are rising?

Answer: Record actual income and expenses using one consistent currency and period. Protect essential needs and legal obligations first, identify flexible spending, and set a realistic saving or debt action. Compare provider terms using total cost, fees, access, risk, and difficult scenarios—not advertising alone. Confirm calculations, keep receipts and statements, protect account credentials, and set a review date. If the decision involves tax, pension, insurance, regulated investment, or a binding credit contract, verify current Liberian rules and obtain qualified assistance before committing.

Summary

What is Financial Literacy? belongs to Introduction to Financial Literacy. A financially capable learner can define it, calculate or compare options, understand risk and total cost, protect information, keep records, and review the decision.

Money habit: Before agreeing, ask: What is the total cost? When is payment due? What can change? What happens if income falls? What evidence and protection do I have?

🛡️ Choosing Insurance Plans

This lesson explains Choosing Insurance Plans so you can identify major risks, understand insurance terms, compare policies, and select appropriate protection. It teaches the definition, calculation or comparison method, risks, and a complete example.

Money decision framework
🛡️ Choosing Insurance Plans
1. Risk
2. Coverage
3. Cost
4. Claim
Amount • timing • total cost • risk • evidence

Definition

Choosing Insurance Plans is a financial-literacy concept or practice used to make informed decisions about money, risk, records, or long-term goals.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Choosing Insurance Plans

Choosing Insurance Plans is a financial-literacy concept or practice used to make informed decisions about money, risk, records, or long-term goals.

premium

the amount paid to keep insurance coverage active

deductible

the amount the insured person must pay before covered insurance benefits begin, according to policy terms

total cost

the full amount paid or used after including price, interest, fees, taxes, maintenance, and other relevant costs

Detailed explanation

Choosing Insurance Plans is a financial-literacy concept or practice used to make informed decisions about money, risk, records, or long-term goals. A sound decision compares the full amount, timing, total cost, uncertainty, access to money, legal terms, and effect on other goals. Records and provider documents matter more than advertising claims.

  • Separate facts from assumptions and promises.
  • Compare at least two realistic options using the same period and basis.
  • Protect essential needs and emergency resilience before taking avoidable risk.
  • Review the plan when income, prices, responsibilities, laws, or goals change.

Step-by-step method

  1. Risk: define the goal, amount, timing, obligations, and information needed.
  2. Coverage: collect statements, contracts, rates, fees, risks, and current rules from reliable sources.
  3. Cost: calculate and compare realistic options, including difficult scenarios.
  4. Claim: choose deliberately, keep records, monitor results, and revise when evidence changes.

Worked real-life example

A family compares what is covered, exclusions, limits, waiting periods, premium, deductible, provider network, claim evidence, and insurer complaint process.

Worked calculation

MeasureMethodExample
Monthly balanceIncome − expensesUS$300 − US$250 = US$50
Savings rateSavings ÷ income × 100US$50 ÷ US$300 × 100 = 16.7%

Check: State currency, period, rate basis, fees, assumptions, and rounding. Provider contracts and current local rules control real transactions.

Common mistakes and corrections

  • Mistake: focusing only on the monthly payment. Correction: compare total repayment, fees, rate, term, penalties, and collateral.
  • Mistake: treating every financial product as guaranteed. Correction: check risk, regulation, provider identity, contract, and loss scenarios.
  • Mistake: mixing personal and business money. Correction: separate accounts, records, budgets, and decisions.
  • Mistake: sharing PINs or one-time codes. Correction: keep credentials private and use official support channels.

Guided practice with detailed answer

Question: How should a learner apply Choosing Insurance Plans when monthly income is limited and expenses are rising?

Answer: Record actual income and expenses using one consistent currency and period. Protect essential needs and legal obligations first, identify flexible spending, and set a realistic saving or debt action. Compare provider terms using total cost, fees, access, risk, and difficult scenarios—not advertising alone. Confirm calculations, keep receipts and statements, protect account credentials, and set a review date. If the decision involves tax, pension, insurance, regulated investment, or a binding credit contract, verify current Liberian rules and obtain qualified assistance before committing.

Summary

Choosing Insurance Plans belongs to Insurance & Risk Management. A financially capable learner can define it, calculate or compare options, understand risk and total cost, protect information, keep records, and review the decision.

Money habit: Before agreeing, ask: What is the total cost? When is payment due? What can change? What happens if income falls? What evidence and protection do I have?

💼 Personal vs. Business Finance

This lesson explains Personal vs. Business Finance so you can separate personal and business money, price correctly, budget, manage cash flow, keep records, and plan sustainably. It teaches the definition, calculation or comparison method, risks, and a complete example.

Money decision framework
💼 Personal vs. Business Finance
1. Separate
2. Cost
3. Price
4. Control
Amount • timing • total cost • risk • evidence

Definition

Separating personal and business finance means maintaining distinct money, accounts, records, budgets, and obligations.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Personal vs. Business Finance

Separating personal and business finance means maintaining distinct money, accounts, records, budgets, and obligations.

gross profit

sales revenue minus the direct cost of goods or services sold

break-even point

the level of sales at which total revenue equals total cost

total cost

the full amount paid or used after including price, interest, fees, taxes, maintenance, and other relevant costs

Detailed explanation

Separating personal and business finance means maintaining distinct money, accounts, records, budgets, and obligations. A sound decision compares the full amount, timing, total cost, uncertainty, access to money, legal terms, and effect on other goals. Records and provider documents matter more than advertising claims.

  • Separate facts from assumptions and promises.
  • Compare at least two realistic options using the same period and basis.
  • Protect essential needs and emergency resilience before taking avoidable risk.
  • Review the plan when income, prices, responsibilities, laws, or goals change.

Step-by-step method

  1. Separate: define the goal, amount, timing, obligations, and information needed.
  2. Cost: collect statements, contracts, rates, fees, risks, and current rules from reliable sources.
  3. Price: calculate and compare realistic options, including difficult scenarios.
  4. Control: choose deliberately, keep records, monitor results, and revise when evidence changes.

Worked real-life example

A small business separates cash, records every sale and expense, calculates full unit cost, sets a price that supports margin, and forecasts when customers pay versus when bills are due.

Worked calculation

MeasureMethodExample
Unit gross profitSelling price − direct unit costUS$10 − US$6 = US$4
Break-even unitsFixed costs ÷ unit contributionUS$200 ÷ US$4 = 50 units

Check: State currency, period, rate basis, fees, assumptions, and rounding. Provider contracts and current local rules control real transactions.

Common mistakes and corrections

  • Mistake: focusing only on the monthly payment. Correction: compare total repayment, fees, rate, term, penalties, and collateral.
  • Mistake: treating every financial product as guaranteed. Correction: check risk, regulation, provider identity, contract, and loss scenarios.
  • Mistake: mixing personal and business money. Correction: separate accounts, records, budgets, and decisions.
  • Mistake: sharing PINs or one-time codes. Correction: keep credentials private and use official support channels.

Guided practice with detailed answer

Question: How should a learner apply Personal vs. Business Finance when monthly income is limited and expenses are rising?

Answer: Record actual income and expenses using one consistent currency and period. Protect essential needs and legal obligations first, identify flexible spending, and set a realistic saving or debt action. Compare provider terms using total cost, fees, access, risk, and difficult scenarios—not advertising alone. Confirm calculations, keep receipts and statements, protect account credentials, and set a review date. If the decision involves tax, pension, insurance, regulated investment, or a binding credit contract, verify current Liberian rules and obtain qualified assistance before committing.

Summary

Personal vs. Business Finance belongs to Entrepreneurship & Business Finance. A financially capable learner can define it, calculate or compare options, understand risk and total cost, protect information, keep records, and review the decision.

Money habit: Before agreeing, ask: What is the total cost? When is payment due? What can change? What happens if income falls? What evidence and protection do I have?

  3. Cash-flow forecast and emergency scenario.
  4. Debt, insurance, and digital-safety review.
  5. Investment-learning plan stating time horizon, risk, diversification, fees, and limitations.
  6. Business section where relevant and a quarterly review schedule.

Assessment rubric

AreaEvidence of quality
AccuracyCalculations reconcile and assumptions, currency, periods, rates, and fees are visible.
FeasibilityActions fit realistic income, obligations, timing, risk, and access.
ProtectionEmergency, insurance, fraud, privacy, and loss scenarios are considered.
ReviewMeasures, records, responsibilities, and review dates are defined.
Important: This project teaches planning. Verify current Liberian laws, taxes, pensions, products, licensing, fees, and protections with the relevant authority or regulated provider before acting.

Module 10: Capstone Project & GraduationComplete lesson

🏆 Certificate of Completion

This lesson explains Certificate of Completion so you can combine goals, budget, saving, protection, debt, investing, business, digital safety, and review into a complete financial plan. It teaches the definition, calculation or comparison method, risks, and a complete example.

Money decision framework
🏆 Certificate of Completion
1. Assess
2. Plan
3. Test
4. Review
Amount • timing • total cost • risk • evidence

Definition

Certificate of Completion is a financial-literacy concept or practice used to make informed decisions about money, risk, records, or long-term goals.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Certificate of Completion

Certificate of Completion is a financial-literacy concept or practice used to make informed decisions about money, risk, records, or long-term goals.

financial plan

a documented strategy connecting current finances, goals, actions, risks, and review dates

assumption

a planning estimate treated as true temporarily and clearly recorded for later review

total cost

the full amount paid or used after including price, interest, fees, taxes, maintenance, and other relevant costs

Detailed explanation

Certificate of Completion is a financial-literacy concept or practice used to make informed decisions about money, risk, records, or long-term goals. A sound decision compares the full amount, timing, total cost, uncertainty, access to money, legal terms, and effect on other goals. Records and provider documents matter more than advertising claims.

  • Separate facts from assumptions and promises.
  • Compare at least two realistic options using the same period and basis.
  • Protect essential needs and emergency resilience before taking avoidable risk.
  • Review the plan when income, prices, responsibilities, laws, or goals change.

Step-by-step method

  1. Assess: define the goal, amount, timing, obligations, and information needed.
  2. Plan: collect statements, contracts, rates, fees, risks, and current rules from reliable sources.
  3. Test: calculate and compare realistic options, including difficult scenarios.
  4. Review: choose deliberately, keep records, monitor results, and revise when evidence changes.

Worked real-life example

The learner builds a fictional or personal plan using private data carefully, tests optimistic and difficult scenarios, states assumptions, and identifies when licensed or qualified advice is needed.

Worked calculation

MeasureMethodExample
Monthly balanceIncome − expensesUS$300 − US$250 = US$50
Savings rateSavings ÷ income × 100US$50 ÷ US$300 × 100 = 16.7%

Check: State currency, period, rate basis, fees, assumptions, and rounding. Provider contracts and current local rules control real transactions.

Common mistakes and corrections

  • Mistake: focusing only on the monthly payment. Correction: compare total repayment, fees, rate, term, penalties, and collateral.
  • Mistake: treating every financial product as guaranteed. Correction: check risk, regulation, provider identity, contract, and loss scenarios.
  • Mistake: mixing personal and business money. Correction: separate accounts, records, budgets, and decisions.
  • Mistake: sharing PINs or one-time codes. Correction: keep credentials private and use official support channels.

Guided practice with detailed answer

Question: How should a learner apply Certificate of Completion when monthly income is limited and expenses are rising?

Answer: Record actual income and expenses using one consistent currency and period. Protect essential needs and legal obligations first, identify flexible spending, and set a realistic saving or debt action. Compare provider terms using total cost, fees, access, risk, and difficult scenarios—not advertising alone. Confirm calculations, keep receipts and statements, protect account credentials, and set a review date. If the decision involves tax, pension, insurance, regulated investment, or a binding credit contract, verify current Liberian rules and obtain qualified assistance before committing.

Summary

Certificate of Completion belongs to Capstone Project & Graduation. A financially capable learner can define it, calculate or compare options, understand risk and total cost, protect information, keep records, and review the decision.

Money habit: Before agreeing, ask: What is the total cost? When is payment due? What can change? What happens if income falls? What evidence and protection do I have?
